_source: NASA NSSDC planetary fact sheets and NASA JPL Solar System Dynamics

_notes.temp_C: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars: mean surface temperature. Gas and ice giants: temperature at the 1 bar pressure level.
_notes.moons: Moon counts for the giant planets keep rising as new small moons are confirmed, so check NASA's current count before quoting a number.

sun.name: Sun
sun.fact: A G-type main-sequence star holding about 99.86% of the Solar System's mass. In roughly 5 billion years it will swell into a red giant.

planets.name: Mercury
planets.fact: Smallest planet. Its surface swings from about 430 °C by day to about -180 °C at night because it has almost no atmosphere.

planets.name: Venus
planets.fact: Hottest planet, hotter than Mercury, because of a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere. A Venus day is longer than its year.

planets.name: Earth
planets.fact: Only place known to host life. About 71% of the surface is ocean.

planets.name: Mars
planets.fact: Home of Olympus Mons, the tallest known volcano in the Solar System (about 22 km high). Evidence shows liquid water once flowed here.

planets.name: Jupiter
planets.fact: More than twice the mass of all other planets combined. The Great Red Spot is a storm that has been observed for well over a century.

planets.name: Saturn
planets.fact: Its rings are mostly water ice and are extremely thin, often only about 10 metres thick in places. Its average density is lower than water.

planets.name: Uranus
planets.fact: Rotates tipped on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees. An ice giant.

planets.name: Neptune
planets.fact: Farthest planet. Measured winds are among the fastest in the Solar System, over 2,000 km/h.

dwarf_planets.name: Pluto
dwarf_planets.fact: Visited by New Horizons in 2015. It has a nitrogen-ice plain called Sputnik Planitia and a huge moon, Charon. Reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

dwarf_planets.name: Ceres
dwarf_planets.fact: The largest object in the asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet in the inner Solar System. Visited by the Dawn spacecraft. Bright spots in Occator crater are salt deposits.

notable_moons.name: Moon
notable_moons.fact: Earth's only natural satellite and the only other world humans have walked on (Apollo, 1969 to 1972). The leading explanation for its origin is a giant impact on the early Earth, which is well supported but still being refined.

notable_moons.name: Io
notable_moons.fact: The most volcanically active body known in the Solar System.

notable_moons.name: Europa
notable_moons.fact: Strong evidence of a salty ocean under its ice shell, which makes it a top target in the search for life. Habitability is unproven.

notable_moons.name: Ganymede
notable_moons.fact: The largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than Mercury, and the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.

notable_moons.name: Titan
notable_moons.fact: Has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. The Huygens probe landed on it in 2005.

notable_moons.name: Enceladus
notable_moons.fact: Cassini flew through plumes of water vapour and ice venting from its south pole, showing a subsurface ocean and organic molecules.

notable_moons.name: Triton
notable_moons.fact: Orbits backwards compared with Neptune's spin, which suggests it was captured from the Kuiper belt.

notable_moons.name: The Moon
notable_moons.fact: About 384,400 km away. Its gravity drives our tides. It most likely formed when a Mars-size body hit the early Earth (the giant-impact hypothesis).
